text.en: Ravi measures the desk with his hand span and gets 7. Meena gets 6. Same desk, different answers! To avoid this we need standard units.

Measurement gives numbers so everyone can agree. Long ago people used a hand span or a foot, but those differ from person to person. So we use standard units, the same for everyone.
The standard unit of length in the SI system is the metre. Smaller lengths use the centimetre and millimetre. Long distances use the kilometre. 1 metre equals 100 centimetres. 1 centimetre equals 10 millimetres. 1 kilometre equals 1000 metres.
Place the ruler along the object with zero at one end. Look straight down at the mark to avoid parallax error. If the end of the ruler is worn, start from a clear mark like 1 cm and subtract. To measure a curved line, lay a thread along it, straighten the thread and measure the thread.
Choose a reference point before describing an object’s motion. If the object’s position relative to that point changes with time, the object is moving relative to that point. A person sitting in a moving bus is at rest for the seat but moving for the road.
Straight line motion is movement along a line, such as a car on a straight road. Circular motion is movement around a fixed point, such as a point on a fan blade. Periodic motion repeats at regular intervals, like a swing or a pendulum. Rotational motion is spinning about an axis, like a top.

board.text: Why measure?

text.en: So we use standard units, the same for everyone.
The standard unit of length in the SI system is the metre. Smaller lengths use the centimetre and millimetre. Long distances use the kilometre.

board.text: Standard units

text.en: 1 metre equals 100 centimetres. 1 centimetre equals 10 millimetres. 1 kilometre equals 1000 metres.
Place the ruler along the object with zero at one end. Look straight down at the mark to avoid parallax error.

board.text: Correct way to measure length

text.en: If the end of the ruler is worn, start from a clear mark like 1 cm and subtract.
To measure a curved line, lay a thread along it, straighten the thread and measure the thread.
Choose a reference point before describing an object’s motion. If the object’s position relative to that point changes with time, the object is moving relative to that point.

board.text: Position and motion

text.en: A person sitting in a moving bus is at rest for the seat but moving for the road.
Straight line motion is movement along a line, such as a car on a straight road.

board.text: Types of motion

text.en: Circular motion is movement around a fixed point, such as a point on a fan blade.
Periodic motion repeats at regular intervals, like a swing or a pendulum.
Rotational motion is spinning about an axis, like a top.
Choose a unit that suits what you are measuring. Centimetres are handy for a pencil, metres for the width of a room, and kilometres for the distance between towns.

board.text: Pencil: cm. Room: m. Towns: km.

text.en: A pencil fifteen centimetres long is also one hundred fifty millimetres long. The number changes because each centimetre contains ten millimetres. The pencil stays the same length.

board.text: 15 cm = 150 mm

text.en: For a trip of two kilometres and three hundred metres, change the kilometres to metres first. Two thousand plus three hundred gives a total of two thousand three hundred metres.
Lay a ruler next to a strip of paper so both run in the same direction. If the ruler’s zero mark is worn, line up one end of the strip with a clear mark instead.

board.text: Line up the ruler with the strip

text.en: Suppose the strip starts at the two-centimetre mark and ends at seven and a half centimetres. Subtract the starting reading. The length of the strip is five and a half centimetres.

board.text: End reading − start reading
7.5 cm − 2 cm = 5.5 cm

text.en: Now place your eye directly above the end mark. From the side, the end can seem to line up with a different graduation if the strip is above the scale.

board.text: Eye above the mark avoids parallax

text.en: Put a unit beside the answer. Writing five and a half centimetres tells a classmate much more than writing five and a half on its own.

board.text: Write the number with its unit

text.en: Draw a curve on paper. Follow it with a piece of thread and mark where the curve starts and ends on that thread. Let the thread follow the bends without loose loops.

board.text: Mark both ends of the curved path

text.en: Lift the thread and lay it straight against a ruler without stretching it. Measure between your two marks. This gives an estimate of the length along the curve.

board.text: Straightened thread gives the curve length

text.en: Put a toy car on a desk and choose a mark on the desk as a reference. At the start the front of the car is at the mark. After a short time it is five centimetres to the right.

board.text: Desk mark: reference point
Position changes from 0 to 5 cm right

text.en: The whole car is moving relative to the desk. A sticker that is stuck on the car stays in the same place relative to the car. The word moving needs a reference to be clear.

board.text: Sticker: moving relative to the desk
Sticker: at rest relative to the car

text.en: Knowing the reference point also helps describe direction. Five centimetres to the right of the desk mark tells you a different position from five centimetres to its left.

board.text: Tell the distance and direction from the mark

text.en: Watch the centre of one wheel on the toy car as the car goes straight. The centre travels along a straight line relative to the desk.

board.text: Wheel centre: straight path on the desk

text.en: Now watch a dot painted beside the edge of that wheel. Relative to the wheel’s centre, the dot travels along a circle as the wheel spins about its axle.

board.text: Dot: circular motion around the axle

text.en: One event can show more than one kind of motion. The wheel rotates, the dot goes around the centre, and the wheel’s centre can move straight along the desk.

board.text: One toy can show several kinds of motion

text.en: Think of a swing moving back and forth. Choose one point in its path. Each time it passes that point in the same direction, one whole cycle has passed since the previous such crossing.

board.text: One cycle: return to the same point and direction

text.en: A motion is periodic when its cycle repeats at regular time intervals. Describe the path and the repeats separately. Circular tells us the shape of a path, while periodic tells us about timing.

board.text: Circular: path
Periodic: timing

text.en: 1 metre is 100 centimetres.
3 times 100 is 300 centimetres.
